## Mathematical derivations/proofs

### Set of positive definite variance covariance matrices for the simulation {#sec-set-pos-definite-vcovs}

As stated in @sec-app-population-simulation, the common covariance matrix $\Sigma$ has the general shape (for the 3 variables case)

$$
\Sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \sigma_{m,1,2} & \sigma_{mh} \\
\sigma_{m,1,2} & 1 & \sigma_{mh} \\
\sigma_{mh} & \sigma_{mh} & 1
\end{pmatrix}
$$ {#eq-general-Sigma-3d}

For notational simplicity let here $a \equiv \sigma_{m,1,2}$ and $b \equiv \sigma_{mh}$.^[
    Note: from here one the derivation has been fully AI-generated with minor changes by me.
    The facts were checked upon by me. See @chatgpt_positive_definite_covariance_2026 for
    the reference to the chat.
]
The space of positive definite covariance matrices following @eq-general-Sigma-3d can be
found using Sylvester's criterion^[
    I.e. if all leading principal minors have a positive determinant, then the matrix is
    positive definite
] and is fully determined by the admissible tuples $(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}^2$.

Using the simplified notation, the covariance matrix can be written as

$$
\Sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & a & b \\
a & 1 & b \\
b & b & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-sigma-ab}

The first leading principal minor always has a positive determinant since $\det(1) = 1 > 0$.
The second leading principal minor is

$$
\det
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & a \\
a & 1
\end{pmatrix}
=
1-a^2.
$$ {#eq-second-principal-minor}

Therefore, the second condition requires

$$
1-a^2 > 0,
$$ {#eq-second-principal-minor-condition}

which is equivalent to

$$
-1 < a < 1.
$$ {#eq-a-range}

Finally, the determinant of the full matrix in @eq-sigma-ab is

$$
\det(\Sigma)
=
\begin{vmatrix}
1 & a & b \\
a & 1 & b \\
b & b & 1
\end{vmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-full-determinant-start}

Subtracting the second row from the first row leaves the determinant unchanged and yields
<!--
Rule applied here: one can add any constant factor of a row to another
without changing the determinant
-->

$$
\det(\Sigma)
=
\begin{vmatrix}
1-a & a-1 & 0 \\
a & 1 & b \\
b & b & 1
\end{vmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-full-determinant-row-operation}

Factoring out $(1-a)$ from the first row gives
<!--
Rule applied here: mutiplying one row with a non zero scalar c of
matrix A, leaves the determinant of the changed matrix
to be c det(A)
https://math.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Linear_Algebra/A_First_Course_in_Linear_Algebra_(Kuttler)/03%3A_Determinants/3.02%3A_Properties_of_Determinants
-->

$$
\det(\Sigma)
=
(1-a)
\begin{vmatrix}
1 & -1 & 0 \\
a & 1 & b \\
b & b & 1
\end{vmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-full-determinant-factorized}

The cofactor expansion results in

$$
\det(\Sigma)
=
(1-a)
\left[
\begin{vmatrix}
1 & b \\
b & 1
\end{vmatrix}
+
\begin{vmatrix}
a & b \\
b & 1
\end{vmatrix}
\right].
$$ {#eq-full-determinant-expansion}

Evaluating the two $2 \times 2$ determinants yields

$$
\det(\Sigma)
=
(1-a)
\left[
(1-b^2) + (a-b^2)
\right].
$$ {#eq-full-determinant-evaluated}

After simplification,

$$
\det(\Sigma)
=
(1-a)(1+a-2b^2).
$$ {#eq-full-determinant}

By @eq-a-range, the factor $(1-a)$ is strictly positive. Consequently, the third condition
of Sylvester's criterion is

$$
1+a-2b^2 > 0.
$$ {#eq-third-principal-minor-condition}

Solving for $b$ gives

$$
b^2 < \frac{1+a}{2},
$$ {#eq-b-condition-squared}

Combining @eq-a-range and @eq-b-condition-squared, the set of positive definite covariance
matrices of the form @eq-general-Sigma-3d is characterized by

$$
\left\{
(a,b)\in\mathbb{R}^2 :
-1<a<1,\;
b^2<\frac{1+a}{2}
\right\}.
$$ {#eq-positive-definite-region}

### On the Bayes Classifier with idiosyncratic shocks

#### Decision boundary {#sec-dec-boundary-perf-bayes-idyiosincratic-shocks}

The decision boundary between two classes is defined as the equal probability
region for both. For our case with two classes there is only one boundary and
it is given by
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=b | X=x) = \mathbb{P}(Y=g | X=x)
$$
$$
\Leftrightarrow \mathbb{P}(Y=b | X=x) = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Plugging in @eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes we get
$$
\pi_{\epsilon} \, p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (b, x) + (1 - \pi_{\epsilon}) \pi_{\varepsilon, b}
= \frac{1}{2}
$$ 
$$
\Leftrightarrow p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (b, x) = \underbrace{\frac{\frac{1}{2} - (1 - \pi_{\epsilon}) \pi_{\varepsilon, b}}{\pi_{\epsilon}}}_{=: \xi}
$$ {#eq-decision-boundary-in-terms-of-clean}

Note that @eq-decision-boundary-in-terms-of-clean shows how considering the idiosyncratic shocks
only moves the decision boundary. If there were no shocks ($\pi_\epsilon = 1$) or their effect
was symmetric $\left(\pi_{\varepsilon, b} = \frac{1}{2} \right)$ then $\xi = \frac{1}{2}$, which
equals the decision boundary based on a classifier ignoring the shocks.

Using @eq-posterior-of-Y, @eq-marginal-of-X and @eq-marginal-of-Y we get
$$
p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (b, x) = \frac{\phi_{X_b}(x) \pi_b}{\pi_b \phi_{X_b}(x) + \pi_g \phi_{X_g}(x)} = \xi
$$
and using $\pi_g = 1 - \pi_b$
$$
\Leftrightarrow  \pi_b(1 - \xi)\phi_{X_b}(x) = \xi (1 - \pi_b) \phi_{X_g}(x)
$$
which allows for a odds ratio perspective
$$
\Leftrightarrow \frac{\phi_{X_b}(x)}{\phi_{X_g}(x)} = \frac{\xi (1 - \pi_b)}{\pi_b(1 - \xi)} =: c
$${#eq-odds-ratio-shock}

Since we assume equal covariances matrices we can get from taking loggs the familiar result
(see e.g. @hastie2009elements, p. 108)
$$
x^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mu_b - \mu_g) - \underbrace{\frac{1}{2} (\mu_b + \mu_g)}_{=:\bar{\mu}} \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_b - \mu_g) =
\log c
$$
After factorizing and using the symmetry of $\Sigma^{-1}$ we get
$$
(\mu_b - \mu_g)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \bar{\mu})  = \log c
$${#eq-decision-boundary-equal-covs}

#### Bayes error rate {#sec-derivation-bayes-rate}

A perfect Bayes classifier considering the idiosyncratic shock as defined in 
@eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes has an analytical solution for the Bayes error.
To get to this expression, I use the results of @Ripley_1996.

For any $\omega \in \Omega$, the decision to classify an applicant as bad with
characteristics $x := X(\omega)$ occurs if
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=b | X = x) > \mathbb{P}(Y=g | X = x)
$$

which following the same steps as before we get an expression like @eq-decision-boundary-equal-covs
that we can use to also define a random variable
$$
A(\omega) := (\mu_b - \mu_g)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x - \bar{\mu}) >
\log c
$$
where, following @Ripley_1996, 
$$
A | Y = b \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\frac{1}{2} \delta^2, \delta^2 \right), \,
A | Y = g \sim \mathcal{N}\left(-\frac{1}{2} \delta^2, \delta^2 \right)
$$
with
$$
\delta = \sqrt{(\mu_b - \mu_g)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (\mu_b - \mu_g)}
$$

Therefore the decision function $d_B$ of the bayes classifier can be written
as
$$
d_B(x) = \begin{cases}
    b & A > \log c \\
    g & A \leq \log c
\end{cases}
$$

The bayes error rate $E_B$ is then given by
$$
\begin{aligned}
E_B &= 
    \mathbb{P}(Y = b) \mathbb{P}(A \leq \log c | Y = b) +
    \mathbb{P}(Y = g)  \mathbb{P}(A > \log c | Y = g)
\\
&=
    \pi_b \Phi\left(-\frac{1}{2}\delta + \frac{1}{\delta} \log c\right) +
    (1-\pi_b) \Phi\left(-\frac{1}{2}\delta - \frac{1}{\delta} \log c\right)
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-bayes-error-rate-formula}

### A possible route towards a formal justification of surprise as a valid signal

The argument in Section @sec-an-unsurprising-setting is intentionally
heuristic. Nevertheless, it is useful to outline how one could
attempt to formalize the claim that surprise should vanish in a
stable MAR environment, which is the sole purpose of this appendix.

Assume the conditions from Section @sec-an-unsurprising-setting hold.
Define the acceptance region at round $t$ as

$$
A_t
:=
\left\{
x \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m}
\;\middle|\;
\hat{s}_t(x) > c_t
\right\}.
$$

The corresponding distribution of accepted applicants is then

$$
\mathbb{P}_{Y,X \mid X \in A_t}(E)
=
\frac{
    \mathbb{P}\left((Y,X)\in E, X\in A_t\right)
}{
    \mathbb{P}\left(X\in A_t\right)
}
$$

for measurable $E \in 2^{E_Y} \otimes \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^f)$.

Suppose additionally that the estimation method is unbiased in the
sense of this thesis, namely that given enough representative data,
the estimated scorecard $\hat{s}_t$ provides a good approximation
of a scoring proportional to $\mathbb{P}(Y=b\mid X)$. Under suitable
regularity conditions and growing sample sizes, one could then
expect the sequence of scorecards $\hat{s}_t$ to stabilize around
some limiting scorecard $s^* \propto \mathbb{P}(Y=b\mid X)$.

Likewise, if the cutoff selection criterion remains unchanged across
rounds, one could expect the sequence of cutoffs $c_t$ to stabilize
around a limiting value $c$. This motivates the introduction of the
limiting acceptance region

$$
A
:=
\left\{
x \in \mathbb{R}^{f_m}
\;\middle|\;
s^*(x) > c
\right\}.
$$

Heuristically, stabilization of $\hat{s}_t$ and $c_t$ suggests that
the acceptance regions $A_t$ become increasingly similar to $A$.
As a consequence, one would expect the distributions of accepted
applicants

$$
\mathbb{P}_{Y,X \mid X \in A_t}
$$

to become increasingly similar across rounds as well.

Although turning this intuition into a rigorous theorem would require
additional assumptions on the estimation method, the applicants
distribution and the acceptance regions, the central idea is simple:
in a stationary MAR environment the acceptance mechanism itself
should eventually stabilize. Once this occurs, both the training
data and future accepted applicants are generated from nearly the
same distribution.

Under such circumstances, one would expect the performance estimated
through cross-validation on historical accepts to be close to the
performance observed on future accepted applicants, implying only
small values of the surprise signal $\eta^{(t)}$.

### Literature Review table

The table @BuckerEtAl2013MNARRI

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import os

path_lit_tbl_xl = "./data/table_literature_review.xlsx"

lit_review_tbl = pd.read_excel(path_lit_tbl_xl)

boolean_cols = lit_review_tbl.columns[lit_review_tbl.dtypes == bool]

boolean_is_true_str = r"$\checkmark$"
boolan_is_false_str = ''

lit_review_tbl[boolean_cols] = lit_review_tbl[boolean_cols].map(lambda x : boolean_is_true_str if x else boolan_is_false_str)

fun_reflbl_to_ref = lambda ref : f"\\cite{{{ref}}}" if False else f"@{ref}"#ref
ref_colname = lit_review_tbl.columns[0]

lit_review_tbl[ref_colname] = lit_review_tbl[ref_colname].apply(fun_reflbl_to_ref)
lit_review_tbl = lit_review_tbl.iloc[:-2]
```
